title: What Does Digital Sovereignty Mean?
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill argues that digital sovereignty is a useful lens for understanding which AI tools education institutions buy, which they resist and what they ask vendors to change. He starts from two events on the same day, the European Commission's approval of pooled EdTech and AI purchasing by eight member states and American voters favouring limits on data-center development in 46 of 47 local measures. After surveying partial and implied definitions he proposes his own: the degree to which a government, community, institution or individual has both the authority and the practical ability to make and revise decisions about the digital technologies it depends on. He asks whose sovereignty is at issue in a given decision, for example an institution disabling AI feedback versus an instructor who designed an assignment around it. He adds that many EdTech products sit on a much smaller set of model providers, so a buyer may hold source code and still lose AI features if the model provider withdraws access.
points: Digital sovereignty combines formal authority with the practical ability to make and revise technology decisions, and both parts are needed.
Always ask whose sovereignty is in play: institutional decisions can remove discretion from instructors or students.
The AI layer complicates the old LMS comparison because buyers often cannot tell which model did the work or control access to it.
European procurement rules and US data-center ballot measures show the same question surfacing in different political forms, which will shape what schools buy.
quotes: On November 3, the European Commission approved a request from eight member states to pool resources for EdTech, including AI tools for schools. One explicit goal was to reduce their dependence on suppliers outside the EU. That same day, American voters favored limits on data-center development in 46 of 47 local ballot measures.

I think digital sovereignty will help explain which AI tools schools buy—both direct contracts with frontier LLMs and embedded AI features in EdTech platforms—which they push back on, and what they ask vendors to change.

As I pull together the various definitions (often partial or implied), I would summarize them as follows: Digital sovereignty is the degree to which a government, community, institution, or individual has both the authority and the practical ability to make and revise decisions about the digital technologies on which it depends.
I would also have the definition do one more job. Whose sovereignty are we talking about? A university that disables AI feedback across all courses has exercised institutional authority.

Then there’s a complication the old LMS comparison misses entirely. There are many EdTech products on the market and a much smaller set of model providers behind them. Sometimes the buyer can’t even establish which model did the work.

Under the proposed act, Article 41 would encourage public bodies to use open standards and openly licensed components. A separate provision would require a public buyer to justify purchasing a cloud service outside the applicable EU assurance level.
The US movement has plenty of top-down politics of its own. Food & Water Watch describes helping residents organize for local moratoria across seven states.
In June I wrote about what changed when Amazon opened its Frankfurt cloud region. Suddenly a university that wanted its data hosted in Germany had an option it could put in a contract.
